pages.title: Slide 2
pages.text:
Why is this Important?
• We’re now experts on the structure of our genetic material
• But, as we should be used to asking by now – so what?!
• Our DNA, and the genes which we find within it, are useless if
  they’re not actually turned into anything – like having lots of
  code on your computer which doesn’t do anything useful!
• So, we’re now going to think about what happens to our gene
  codes to give us amino acid sequences - we should know how
  important they are!
• Knowing how this works is important – it allows us to
  understand disease, and to target drugs to stop these
  processes – this can be really useful!

pages.title: Slide 6
pages.text:
Knowing this is Important!

• This is all nice and simple so far, but knowing the basics of this overall
  process is critical
• It’s how we manufacture our proteins!
• Without these processes, we wouldn’t have proteins, and without
  proteins, we wouldn’t have us!
• These processes allow different proteins to exist:
     • Each with their own amino acid sequence…
     • …with that sequence being coded for by mRNA…
     • …which is coded for by a gene in our DNA!
• So, let’s get into the detail – starting with the first step: TRANSCRIPTION

media.webLabel: Open slide 6 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 7
pages.text:
Gene Transcription and Translation

Part 1. Transcription

media.webLabel: Open slide 7 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 8
pages.text:
Transcription – Coding DNA into mRNA!

• We know the basics of the process of transcription
• The conversion of a gene’s code into mRNA
• But what is mRNA?
• mRNA is messenger ribonucleic acid
• It’s a single-stranded code which takes the message from a gene
  to another location in the cell, outside the nucleus, for translation
  into a protein – we’ll talk more about translation later!
• Think of it as the go-between used by our DNA, and the tools in our
  cell that make proteins from a provided code

pages.title: Slide 10
pages.text:
Transcription – Let’s Get Going!

• We’re now at a point where we know what we want to happen, and
  we’ve got the main tools needed to do this
• When it comes to transcription, there are three main steps to
  consider:
   1. Initiation
   2. Elongation
   3. Termination
• At the end of these three steps, we’ll have a nice piece of mRNA
  which can be translated into a sequence of amino acids!

media.webLabel: Open slide 10 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 11
pages.text:
Step 1: Initiation
• Initiation gets underway when RNA polymerase (an enzyme)
  attaches to a section of the DNA called the promoter
• The first job RNA polymerase does is to unwind the DNA, exposing
  the bases which are in one of the strands called the template
  strand - it’ll expose about 20-30 bases at any one time
• The RNA polymerase is now ready to read that strand that it has
  exposed!

media.webLabel: Open slide 11 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 12
pages.text:
Step 2: Elongation
• RNA polymerase is involved here too!
• In this stage, it’ll read along the exposed part of the DNA template strand – this
  is called a transcription bubble
• As it does this, it’ll bring over RNA nucleotides to the template, which are
  complementary for the DNA nucleotide, connecting these together
• The DNA will wind back up behind the RNA polymerase, reforming the double
  helix – this keeps the DNA stable and protected!

                                                                          Transcription
                                                                             bubble

media.webLabel: Open slide 12 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 13
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Which way is the copy made?
pages.text:
Elongation – Directions are Important!
• RNA polymerase will read the TEMPLATE strand of the DNA in the 3’ to 5’
  direction
• mRNA is synthesised in the 5’ to 3’ direction – the 5’ end of the mRNA chain is
  what extends away from the site of mRNA synthesis




                           RNA polymerase moves this way

media.webLabel: Open slide 13 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Which way is the copy made?
practice.prompt: A student draws two arrows pointing in the same direction and says both the template and the new RNA are read or built from 5′ to 3′. How would you label the two directions for transcription?
practice.answer: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template from 3′ to 5′. The new RNA is synthesised from 5′ to 3′. The labels refer to different strands and actions.

pages.title: Slide 16
pages.text:
Understanding the Strands

• Earlier, you might remember we mentioned the template
  strand of the DNA
• This is what the mRNA nucleotides bind to by
  complementary base pairing
• The template strand is the strand which doesn’t contain the
  gene’s code, but which does match with it!
• This means that if the mRNA nucleotides bind to the
  template strand, the resulting chain of mRNA nucleotides
  will be a copy of the gene (except the Ts are Us)

media.webLabel: Open slide 16 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 17
pages.text:
The coding and template strands run in opposite directions. For this diagram the RNA sequence, read 5′ to 3′, follows the coding strand with uracil in place of thymine.

pages.title: Slide 18
pages.text:
Step 3: Termination

• We eventually get to the point where the gene has been transcribed
  into its single-stranded mRNA code
• But remember, there is lots of DNA before and after each gene
• Termination is what allows the mRNA manufacture to stop, making
  sure that it contains the right code, of the right length!
• This process occurs when the RNA polymerase reaches a specific
  sequence of DNA called the termination sequence
• Termination happens when RNA polymerase reaches a specific
  sequence that signals the end of transcription – this releases the
  mRNA, which is then further processed by specialised enzymes!

media.webLabel: Open slide 18 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 19
pages.text:
…and that’s it! Not really…
• We now know how a strand of messenger RNA is formed, which is great!
• But, things are much more complicated than this!
• Remember that each single stand within the DNA molecule contains LOTS of
  genes – many of these are being transcribed at the same time – if we only did
  one gene at a time, we’d have some problems!
• It’s also important to remember that both DNA strands from a double-stranded
  DNA molecule are involved in transcription – the templates for some genes are
  on one strand, and others are on the other strand!
• Further to that, if we need lots of a particular protein, we can see multiple RNA
  polymerase molecules binding to a single gene at the same time, so that we
  can make lots of mRNA, and ultimately, lots of protein! When this happens,
  we’ll see multiple transcription bubbles on the same gene!

media.webLabel: Open slide 19 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.text: Two transcription bubbles appear on one stretch of double-stranded DNA. RNA polymerase uses opposite strands as templates for the two pictured genes, and the arrows for transcription point in opposite directions.

Gene Transcription and Translation

Part 2. Processing the Transcript

media.webLabel: Open slide 21 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 22
pages.jumpLabel: Processing Gives us the Final mRNA
pages.text:
Processing Gives us the Final mRNA
Code

• At this point, we’ve taken the code for the gene in the
  template strand of the DNA, and turned this into a single
  mRNA strand
• But at the moment, it’s still not quite ready to do its job and
  be translated into a sequence of amino acids – some more
  processing is required!

media.webLabel: Open slide 22 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 23
pages.text:
What About the Introns?!

• If we think back to what we know about DNA, we know that genes
  contain exons and introns – the introns are non-coding
• But – their code is included in the mRNA transcript – which is a
  problem!
• So, we need to get rid of the introns from our transcript before it can
  be translated into the amino acid sequence we need!

media.webLabel: Open slide 23 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 24
pages.text:
A pre-mRNA contains two exons on either side of an intron. During splicing the intron loops out and is removed; the exons join in the mature messenger RNA.

RNA Splicing

               These are
                  then
               destroyed!

practice.title: Tracking a missing segment
practice.prompt: An initial transcript has three consecutive regions. The first and third sit next to one another in the mature transcript. Which processing event explains the changed arrangement, and which material changed?
practice.answer: The middle region was an intron in the RNA. During splicing it was removed and the flanking exons were joined. The diagram shows RNA processing, so the change described is in the transcript.

pages.title: Slide 25
pages.text:
…and that’s it! Sort of…

• We’re now at the point where we have our finished,
  polished mRNA transcript
• We’ve got the copy of the gene’s code that we need to tell
  the cell (our computer) how to place amino acids together
  in a particular sequence which will then give us the protein
  which the gene codes for
• That protein can then go on and do whatever its job is!
• But how does that software turn into a protein? Via the
  process of translation!

media.webLabel: Open slide 25 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 26
pages.text:
Gene Transcription and Translation

Part 3. Translating the Code

media.webLabel: Open slide 26 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 27
pages.text:
Understanding the Code
• Before we can translate a language, we need to understand the basics of how
  it works
• The same is true of the code which is held in our mRNA
• One of the keys to understanding this coding language is the codon – which
  we should know about already!
• These codons are sequences of THREE nucleotides in the mRNA sequence
  which generally code for a particular amino acid
• Those codons originally came from the DNA of the gene in question
• So, if a particular codon is present at a particular part of the mRNA sequence,
  then the amino acid it codes for will be present at the equivalent position in the
  protein which is produced!
• This means that the individual nucleotides don’t code for things on their own,
  but instead form “words” which can be understood!

practice.title: Two kinds of punctuation
practice.prompt: A classmate says that a start signal and a stop signal must each contribute one amino acid to the chain. Which part of the claim needs revising? Give evidence from the codon slides.
practice.answer: The start codon AUG specifies methionine in this example. A stop codon tells the translation machinery to end the chain and adds no amino acid. Compare pages 29 and 30.

               • If we need a codon to stop the process,
                 we need one to start it too!
               • We have a single start codon – AUG

                 Methionine
               • This means that immature proteins

The Translation Hardware


• We now have the mRNA code that we need…
• …and the dictionary which we need to understand that
  code
• All we need now is hardware which can read the code and
  put things together
• There are two main bits – the ribosome and the transfer
  RNA (tRNA)!

practice.title: Matching the message to its cargo
practice.prompt: A diagram labels a three-base sequence on mRNA and another on a molecule carrying an amino acid. Both labels currently say codon. How would you relabel the drawing so the relationship is clear?
practice.answer: The sequence on mRNA is a codon and the complementary sequence on tRNA is an anticodon. Their pairing connects the message to the amino acid carried by the tRNA.

pages.title: Slide 35
pages.text:
…and that’s it! Not Yet (sorry!)…

• After all that, we now have our initial sequence of amino acids – the
  PRIMARY PROTEIN STRUCTURE!
• But we know that this isn’t the end of the story for proteins – this
  gives us our secondary, tertiary, and even quaternary structures!
• Further to all of that, we’ll see a range of post-translational
  modifications taking place which help form the final structure of
  proteins, allowing them to carry out their function within our cells
  and elsewhere – you’ll find out more about these on Canvas!

media.webLabel: Open slide 35 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 36
pages.text:
To Sum Up…

• We’ve now gone from the DNA code that we have in our genes,
  which we covered in our first lecture…
• …to the formation of an intermediate code in the form of mRNA…
• …we know how this is processed to give us some computer code…
• …which the ribosome and tRNA hardware can read…
• …in reading this code, amino acids are brought together in a
  particular sequence, giving us the starting point of the protein in
  question!
• Easy!

media.webLabel: Open slide 36 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 37
pages.text:
Next Time…

• We’ll start to think about the fact that not all of our
  genes are being transcribed and translated all the time
• In fact only some cells need certain proteins…
• …and we only need certain proteins at certain times!
• To make this work, your body controls transcription
  tightly – we’ll talk about how this happens, keeping
  everything balanced!
